personas.name: Maria, front desk clerk
personas.summary: Runs the front desk: takes bookings, and checks guests in and out.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To tell a guest at once whether a room is free for their dates, and hold it
  for them, without ever giving the same room to two guests.
- To check guests in and out quickly, so nobody waits at the desk.
- To know which rooms are ready before a guest arrives, without phoning
  housekeeping.

## Knows

Every room in the hotel, the regulars, and the cancellation policy by heart.
Comfortable with a computer, but has learned the system on the job, not from a
manual.

## Context

At the desk all shift, on a shared desktop, with a guest or the phone waiting
most of the time. Interrupted constantly, so anything they start may be
finished minutes later.

## Expects

The paper diary's view of the hotel: rooms down the side, nights across the
top. Talks about stays, rooms and arrivals, not reservations or inventory.

## Cares about

Never having to tell a guest standing in front of them that their room was
given away. They'll go back to the paper diary the first time the app gets
that wrong.

personas.name: Ana, housekeeper
personas.summary: Cleans and readies the rooms between guests.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To know which rooms to clean first, so arriving guests don't wait for a
  room.
- To tell the front desk a room is ready without walking back down to say so.

## Knows

The building, floor by floor, and how long each kind of room takes. Uses a
phone every day, but rarely for work.

## Context

On their feet, moving from room to room with a trolley, a phone in their pocket.
Gloves on much of the time, so anything they do has to take a tap or two.

## Expects

A list of rooms, in the order they'll do them. Talks about rooms being clean,
dirty or ready.

## Cares about

Not being rushed by the front desk for a room they didn't know was urgent.

personas.name: David, hotel manager
personas.summary: Runs the hotel, and answers for its takings to the owners.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To set what each room costs, night by night, so busy dates earn more.

## Knows

The local market and the hotel's busy seasons. Reads a spreadsheet well, and
expects software to do the arithmetic for them.

## Context

At a desk in the back office, a few times a week, in between everything else
running a hotel brings.

## Expects

A calendar of rates, like the one they keep in a spreadsheet today.

## Cares about

Rates they can change in a minute when a big event is announced, and being sure
the front desk is quoting them.

concepts.name: Booking
concepts.summary: A guest's hold on one room for a stay, from a check-in date to a check-out date.
concepts.body:
## Details

A booking is for one [room](room.md). Its nights run from the check-in date up
to, but not including, the check-out date.

## Lifecycle

Confirmed → Checked in → Checked out

A confirmed booking can instead be Cancelled, any time before check-in.

concepts.name: Room
concepts.summary: A room guests can stay in, known by its number.
concepts.body:
## Details

Each room has a type, such as double or twin, which sets its rate. A room is
[booked](booking.md) a night at a time.

gaps.text: When every room is taken there's no waitlist. Clerks note the guest's details outside the app and call them if a room frees up.
A booking holds one room, so a family that needs two rooms makes two bookings.
The room calendar can't be used from the keyboard, so clerks need a mouse to pick dates.
The late-cancellation fee isn't charged yet, so every cancellation is refunded in full.

categories.name: Utility
categories.why: It's worth building, and this is the right way to build it.

items.expect: Those judging the idea can try it, or watch it run, enough to tell whether it's worth doing and whether this is the way to do it.

examples.text: A clickable UI with fake or hard-coded data.

notYet: Polishing anything the idea doesn't depend on.
Building out the parts of the system that aren't the question.

items.expect: It works end to end on the real system and is used for real, and what's learned shapes what comes next.

examples.text: Wired to real storage and services, with sample data where real data isn't needed.
A few people, teams, or systems using it for real work, or a job running on a real schedule.
Whether it's being used, and how, is recorded.
Notes on what worked and what didn't, feeding the next round of changes.

notYet: Settling its shape. Big changes are still expected.

items.expect: The need and the solution are confirmed, so what changes from here is refinement, and what success looks like is agreed.

examples.text: Success measures agreed with whoever asked for it, such as adoption, time saved, error rates, or jobs completed.

items.expect: Shown to deliver what it's for in real use.

examples.text: Usage or outcome numbers that meet the measures agreed at Beta.

categories.name: Usability

examples.text: In-app help, or a guide to the main tasks.

Consistent status codes, and error bodies that say what went wrong without exposing internals.

Confirmation, undo, or a dry run before anything destructive.

Dates, times, numbers, and languages shown the way its users expect.

A shared design system, so screens look and behave the same way.

How to install, upgrade, and troubleshoot it.

Handling edge cases or bad input.

items.expect: The main path is known to work after every change, and errors are visible, never silent.

examples.text: End-to-end tests of the main path's happy path, through the public interface, with real dependencies.
A request to each endpoint gets the response it should.
The main flow, driven through the UI.
Run each command on a fixture, and check its output and exit code.
Run it on sample input, and check what it wrote.
The common flows a consumer follows, through its public API.
Acceptance tests for the core rules it follows, annotated with `docket:verifies`.
Tests run on every change, and a failure blocks merging.
Input validated where it enters.

notYet: Unit and integration tests for edge cases, coverage targets, load tests.

items.expect: Unusual input and error paths are handled correctly, and are known to stay that way as it changes.

examples.text: Unit tests for logic, edge cases, and failure paths, such as empty, missing, duplicate, and oversized input.

Acceptance tests for its edge-case rules too.

End-to-end tests of the main flows and their error states.
For output that varies from run to run, such as an AI feature's, quality judged against a set of examples.
Data validated before it's written.

items.expect: Every critical workflow is known to work after every change, and a fixed bug stays fixed.

examples.text: End-to-end tests for every critical workflow.
A regression test with each bug fix.

No flaky or skipped tests left untracked.

categories.name: Reliability
categories.why: It keeps working, and recovers when something goes wrong.

examples.text: Fake, hard-coded, or in-memory data, local files, or a throwaway database.

notYet: Migrations, backups, retries, failover.

examples.text: Real storage, with data that may be reset, and those using it know that.
A script to reset or seed its data.

notYet: Migrations that preserve data, backups, rollback plans.

items.expect: Data that people or systems put in is kept across changes, a bad release can be undone, and when something it depends on is slow or down, it fails clearly or degrades gracefully instead of hanging.

examples.text: Versioned migrations run by the release, never by hand.
A down migration, or a backup taken before a risky change.
A rollback to the previous release.
A quick fixed release.
It can be switched off quickly without a release, such as with a kill switch.
Timeouts on every call to a dependency, with retries only where they're safe.
Local data migrated on upgrade.
Files it wrote can still be read after an upgrade.

notYet: Restore drills, chaos testing, running in several regions.

items.expect: It holds up under overlapping runs, partial failures, and retries, and meets its availability target. Recovering from a bad release or a loss of data is known to work.

examples.text: Operations safe to repeat, such as with idempotency keys or upserts.
Tests for two runs at once, and for retrying after a crash halfway through.
It fails safe where failing could cause harm, stopping rather than charging twice, sending twice, or acting on bad data.
An agreed availability target, such as 99.9%, that's measured.
A rollback that's been practiced, including upgrading, downgrading, and upgrading again.
Automated backups, with a restore that's been tested.
Migrations tried on production-sized data before they ship.
Rerunning a time range rebuilds what it produced.

examples.text: Fast enough that those trying it can judge the idea.

notYet: Optimizing, caching, load testing.

examples.text: Fix what's slow enough to get in the way of real use.

notYet: Load tests, caches, scaling work.

items.expect: Works at realistic volumes, and the work it does is bounded.

examples.text: Tried with realistic amounts of data and use.
No query or call for each item in a list, and indexes where queries need them.
Paging, input size limits, and streaming instead of loading everything into memory.
Limits on what it accepts and returns are documented.
Finishes well within its schedule at realistic volumes.
Starts quickly.
Usable on a slow connection.

items.expect: Meets agreed targets for speed and cost at peak load, with headroom, and its limits are known.

examples.text: Measured targets for response time, throughput, or how long a job takes.
A load test at expected peak, with room to spare.
The rate limits and quotas of what it depends on fit peak use.

Memory, battery, and data use fit the devices it runs on.

categories.name: Security
categories.why: Systems and data are protected the same way at every level, and it follows the rules that apply to it.

items.expect: Secrets stay out of code, version control, sample data, logs, and output. Real data comes only through the real systems, never copied into code or fixtures. Only those allowed can reach real systems or data, and one tenant or account never sees or changes another's. Personal data is collected only where it's needed. Untrusted input can't run as code or commands.

examples.text: Secrets in the environment or a secret store.
Sample data that's made up, not exported from production.
Every read and write scoped to the tenant or account making it.
Established libraries for authentication and cryptography, never hand-rolled ones.
Parameterized queries, escaped output, and no shell commands built from input.

items.expect: It depends on nothing less stable than itself, and its dependencies are maintained and licensed for how it's used.

examples.text: Nothing it relies on is at an earlier stability level, such as a prototype service, or a third party's preview API.
Licenses checked when a dependency is added.
Dependency versions pinned, such as with a lock file.

notYet: Security reviews, compliance audits.

items.expect: Protected against misuse at the level it's exposed, and the legal and regulatory duties that apply are known and met.

examples.text: Authentication on every endpoint, rate limits, and input size limits.
Protection against cross-site request forgery.
The checks in OWASP ASVS level 1.
What it receives is checked for who sent it, such as signed webhooks.
Known vulnerabilities in dependencies found and fixed.
Privacy duties met, such as exporting or deleting someone's personal data on request.
Rules about where data may be stored, and for how long.

items.expect: Its handling of credentials, payments, personal data, and permissions is known to be sound. Each part has only the access it needs, and sensitive actions can be traced to who did them.

examples.text: A security review of sign-in and permission checks.
The checks in OWASP ASVS level 2.
Service accounts and tokens limited to what each part needs.
An audit log of sensitive actions.
Data and logs kept no longer than they're needed.
Builds that can be traced to their source, with a list of what's in them, such as SLSA provenance and an SBOM.
Signed releases.
A penetration test, where the risk warrants one.

categories.name: Compatibility
categories.why: It works with the systems, platforms, and standards around it, and doesn't break those depending on it as it changes.

items.expect: It reaches only those who chose to try it, is marked with its stability level, and can be removed without affecting anything people rely on.

examples.text: Behind a feature flag that's off by default.
A separate environment, or a preview deploy.
A preview endpoint, or an experimental command or flag.
An experimental module, or a pre-release version.
A prototype or alpha label wherever it's used.

Semantic HTML, with native controls before custom ones.
The language's packaging conventions, and semantic versioning.
Standard schedule syntax, such as cron expressions.
Opt-in for invited people or systems, still behind a flag.
Breaking changes made freely, with those trying it told.

items.expect: It's available to everyone it's meant for, without opting in, on the platforms and environments it supports. Those depending on it hear about changes, and breaking ones are rare and announced ahead of time where possible.

items.expect: Its interface is stable, with breaking changes as a new version and the old one kept working for a set time, and it's known to work on every platform it supports.

examples.text: Semantic versioning, with deprecation warnings before removal.
